about: Round 3 of booklet candidates (26 November 2026), planned under the family cap as changed that day (evals/README.md, "Changes to the criteria"): 8 variants where every variant's answer is worked out afresh from its own numbers (numbers, rankings, labels, statements that differ only in their numbers), 4 otherwise, never more than 2 at one letter. Every new variant's answer letter is fixed here so that no letter exceeds 2 in its family; its currency is fixed so that the round moves the bank towards the booklets' mix. Sources that failed before are limited or left out (`left out` below). Before writing: delete the 9 dropped round-2 leftovers from content/candidates (the stopping rule; their letters are not reused), and check that the app keeps siblings apart in sessions and mocks (the precondition for any fifth variant). Groups 1 to 8: 140 candidates for about 135 admitted. Groups 9 to 12 (added the same day, README "The keyed claim"): 64 candidates in 16 statement families already at 4, each new variant keying a different one of its source's claims from the one the admitted siblings key (`keys`, from the source's `keyedClaim.claims`), so that no claim is keyed by more than 4 variants (half of 8); about 50 admitted. Groups 13 and 14 (added later that day): the six statement families written to 4 in groups 1 to 8, opened the same way (24 candidates; their waiting variants carry `keys` under `waiting`), and the last single slots in four numeric families (4). bk-pracB-q09-d and -e were never written (D is unreachable). 230 candidates written or planned, about 205 admitted: about the 200 wanted, if the moved-key variants pass at about 80%.
currencyRule: Dollars, euros or pounds as each variant's `currency` says; `none` where the source names no currency. Pounds only for sources in pounds (pracA-q22, pst1-q14, pst2-q14); euros for sources in euros and for some dollar sources, set in an unnamed country where euros are plausible. Never name a real country, the UK included (WRITING.md section 4: at most an invented or unnamed country); one currency per question.

sources.note: Share of a preparation cost explained by a weight loss valued at the purchase price, from a labelled waterfall ($ per kg, two decimals), closest. Keep the loose premise and the 20/30/40/50% grid (the siblings kept it too); the 40% trap applies the loss to the wrong price. Answer at A needs the true share near 20% with the trap still on a higher option. Siblings passed first time.

New source. Average daily tonnage Monday to Friday from a line chart read from gridlines (7 days shown), best approximates. Traps: dividing by 7 (always below, so not A), leaving out Friday, averaging the two end days. Answers must survive quarter-step readings. Its chart is the worked example's (pracC-q21, evals/calibration/faithful.json): take nothing from that example's setting or numbers.

Profit per item after a 10% rise: (sum of three category profits x 1.1) / items, in millions. Options pair each value with its ten-times slip, not ascending: copy the pattern; answer exact to the unit. The source is in pounds: these in pounds, country unnamed.

Ranks five quintiles by percentage fall from a labelled two-series horizontal bar chart (quintile 5 at the top); every option starts with the same quintile. Traps: ranking by level, a neighbouring bar. Reword past "What is the correct ranking of the five quintiles in Exhibit 1". Limited to 3: two siblings needed the fix round.

"Most likely TRUE" among statements on a 9x3 table by contact level, segment and size; two notCovered and one no-basis statement as the source has; 93% surplus. Cap stays 4 (the keyed claim is the same in every variant); the last slot answers at B.

ROI hurdle statements: one option's annual return sets the rate the other must beat; options in pairs (maximum / minimum amount, at least / at most rate), the "minimum" one a filler; the loose "at least" key, keep. Same table as the worked example pst2-q05: avoid faithful.json's setting. Cap stays 4; the last slot answers at A. The source is in euros.

Ranks four countries by volatility = max - min growth (negative minima). The risk-letter and corruption rows are surplus and offer a rival ranking; the one trap ranks by the minimum alone; two filler rankings as the source has. Siblings passed first time.

Approximate % change in items per day (items / days per period); four paired options (3% / 5%, fewer / more); "than in any of the other months" is loose, keep; skipping the per-day step gives the 3% trap. Siblings passed first time.

Share of the whole customer base giving ratings 1 to 3 = sum of three slices x respondents' share of the base; four pies, one used; options unordered with a ten-times slip, the "1 and 2 only" slip and one filler.

Maximum hours in-house staff may take so the switch pays: (outsourcing + defect fixing on one line) / hourly wage, keyed as the largest option not above it (best check, at-most score). Keep the options in no order and the second line and other wage unused. Limited to 2: bk-bcg-q14-a failed because counting the other product line too still picked its answer; check that slip (both lines, or the other line's subcontractor cost) lands on a wrong option.

Average revenue per analyst = total revenue / total analysts over twelve items from two labelled bar charts. Options not ascending (a ten-times slip beside the answer); traps leave one revenue bar or one analyst bar out of its total; dropping a small bar must not land on the answer unless slipsOnAnswer lists it. Limited to 2: three of four siblings needed the fix round.

Which idea LEAST improves minutes per unit, with FTE read from a step-joined scatter by output band; all 12 values on gridlines; keep the "a total of 3 extra" robustness. Cap stays 4; the last slot answers at B.

Percentage-point difference between two periods' profit margins from a monthly-averages table; days and items rows unused. The source records no trap (three fillers, options 1.5 points apart): none is required; declare any real slip. Invented country (Molvania is a booklet name). Siblings passed first time.

Maximum extra price for a new machine whose labour and electricity savings repay within three years; cents per kWh to dollars. No trap recorded (a tight even $10 grid): none required. Small figures like the source's.

Average order value over two pack sizes: price per litre x volume x units per order, averaged; the discount threshold is not reached (the trap). Options in the source's pattern (value, five times, next value, five times), closest. Siblings passed first time.

Difference in average monthly profit between two periods (revenue x margin; revenue - cost agrees within rounding). Two traps (margin points x one revenue; margin read on costs) and a bottom filler; answer at A is unproven, so B, C, D. The source is in euros.

Statements on a scatter of margin against share (gridlines): a margin ratio "approximately N times"; two notCovered. Keep the looseness but no quarter-step reading may flip it. Cap stays 4; the last slot answers at B.

Highest litres per head = cups per head x cup size across four countries (Country A to D). Cost and price columns unused; two slips land on the answer in the source (slipsOnAnswer); the rounding trap needs two products close. Keep it this light.

Extra items handled by hand = (1 - machine share) x items, difference between periods, from a flow table and a volume table; the middle flow rows are distractors. One trap (the fall in machine-handled items) and two fillers in an even grid.

Difference in respondents giving one rating when one group is three times the other: % x N for each, subtract; four charts, one criterion used. Options evenly spaced; C is new to the family: the "reports one count without subtracting" slips must still land on wrong options.

Percentage-point difference in awareness between two customer groups from a survey table; traps read a usage row, the considered row, or mixes rows. Both new variants answer at B, which no sibling has: put the considered-row difference above the true difference and below the mixed-row slip. If the traps cannot all be kept with B, write one and report it. Pilot family, passed.

Average annual market-share loss over three year-steps from a line chart read from gridlines, closest, in percentage points. Traps: the wrong series, the total instead of the annual loss (always above, so not D); the filler continues the spacing; counting four years lands near the answer in the source too (slipsOnAnswer).

Tier 1: the rating with the most responses over two questions put to the same respondents = sum of percentages, from four labelled pies, two unused. Options are the ratings 1 to 4, so the answer can be any rating; the three traps (one question alone, the fewest, the other area) must land on the other three. Keep tier 1. Siblings passed first time.

Cost of one group = difference of two cumulative % from a labelled cumulative chart x total cost (fixed + attendances x variable cost), closest. Traps read the wrong bar's increment; options evenly spaced. The source is in pounds: write these in pounds, country unnamed.

Approximate change in profit per item between two periods; four paired options (about 20% / 40%, less / more); the trap reverses the direction, the other two are fillers. The source is in euros. Siblings passed first time.

Ranks five of twelve items by revenue per analyst from two labelled horizontal bar charts; seven items unused; traps swap the close pair, rank by headcount, or read an adjacent bar. Keep the full-time caveat sentence. Limited to 3: two siblings needed the fix round.
Profit in one market = market size x share x margin read from a scatter (gridlines), closest. Forgetting the margin gives sales, far above, so the answer sits at A or B only; the one open slot is B.

GDP x summed indirect contribution points = amount attributed; loose premise (ten-year points on current GDP), keep; evenly spaced grid (wideGrid), no trap required. Invent the country; 2013/2023 is the source's year pair.

Ranks four risks by probability x cost from a scatter read from gridlines, closest. Traps: by cost alone, by probability alone, one cost misread off the gridlines. Siblings all answered A or D; these answer at B and C (rankings can sit at any letter). Pilot family, passed.
Minutes per unit = FTE x 160 hours x 60 / units for two periods, difference, closest. Evenly spaced wide grid (sourceHas wideGrid), no trap required; keep the 50% time share in prose.

Second-largest market = step between the first two bars of a 50-bar cumulative chart read from gridlines x total, closest. The cumulative-height trap is always above the answer, so not D. Options as far apart as the source's; keep the groups field and about 9 of 50 values on gridlines. Limited to 2: all three siblings needed the fix round.

Tier 1: ranks four companies by profit per product in one category; the two traps swap the two rows with equal product counts; one filler ranking, never two. Limited to 2: the pilot's four failed on the filler, and bk-pst2-q15-c failed with two rankings no slip produces.

Ranks five quintiles by revenue per transaction from a table; the one-year-value chart is surplus. Keep the near tie (the source's $85 against $86) as the trap and a stem that does not start "What is the correct ranking of the five quintiles in Exhibit". All four admitted siblings passed every judge first time.

Annual cost comparison: tiered price (first N kg at one rate, the rest lower) against a flat price; four paired options (+/- X, +/- 2X); the "other costs" line is unused; the tier break stays below the annual volume. Siblings passed first time.

Projected profit of one category against another as half / the same / twice / three times, growing revenue at past rates with fixed margins. Keep near-equal growth (rates a point or two apart) so base-year profits give the answer, and the "three times" top step as the source's filler. Pilot family.

Tier 1: respondents in a sub-branch = total x share x share from two labelled pies. Every wrong option is a slip (wrong slice, skipping the first pie); skipping the first pie always gives more, so the answer cannot be D. Keep tier 1. Siblings passed first time.

Average of yearly revenue per salesperson over the last four years from two line charts read from gridlines (one dual-axis), closest; options in no order with ten-times slips. Limited to 2: bk-pst2-q21-d failed (one option had no slip within 5%, and the other segment's line nearly landed on the answer): every option needs its slip within 5%, and the other line must land well away.

Visitors per day x share who come once; four sentences that differ only in the number. Rounding 365 to 400 always gives less and the two-slip option more, so the answer sits at B, or at C when the share rounds down; one slot left (C). Invent the setting.

Ranks five of nine units by result / cost from two labelled horizontal bar charts; four units unused (one is the client's own, used by pracA-q23). Traps: ranking by the result alone, swapping the close pair (the source's 8.3 against 8.1), the reversed order. The source is in pounds and all four siblings used dollars: write these in pounds, country unnamed. Round 2 revised 3 of 4 in the fix round (all then passed): check each trap ranking really follows its slip.

Probability that a random visit was a person's only visit = once-only people / total visits; options 25/33/66/75% (66 not 67, keep). Traps: wrong base (repeat visits), share of people, the complement. No national institutions. Siblings passed first time.

Year with the highest segment profit as % of total sales: sales = total profit / margin from bar notes. Labelled stacked bar with negative segments and two barNoteRows; keep negatives. Siblings all answered A or D; these answer at B and C (the source's own answer is C): the total-margin and profit-base traps must land on other years.
Highest income in dollars = local income / exchange rate (label options). The PPP row is unused and the trap; one filler label. Limited to 3: all three siblings needed the fix round.

Which statement can be concluded from a two-company table of percentages; per-outlet volume is the only computable one; three notCovered allowed, one no-basis. Cap stays 4; the last slot answers at B.

Statements on a three-line indexed chart read from gridlines: proportionality and shares of hours; one notCovered; keep the key robust to quarter-step readings. Cap stays 4; the last slot answers at B.

Statements on shares of a combined pair of units from a 100% stacked bar read from gridlines; the keyed multi-category statement must hold for every quarter-step reading, and a single-unit reading must not make another option true (why bk-pst3-q20-b failed). Cap stays 4; the last slot answers at A. Pilot family.

sources.note: Which 1% (or 2%) change most raises profit, given that one cost rises in line with revenue. All siblings keyed the cut in that in-line cost, the largest base. e and g key the revenue rise: a business whose in-line cost is under half of revenue (a software or media firm paying, say, 30% in royalties), so revenue minus the in-line cost beats every cost base; the slip "the largest cost is the biggest lever" now leads to the in-line cost. f and h key the other main cost: it is larger than the in-line cost (a labour-heavy service with small pass-through costs); forgetting that revenue drags the in-line cost with it leads to the revenue rise. The smaller cost stays dominated. Two trapped wrong options.
